MM 04:
Her mom told her she'd be assaulted — and that she'd deserve it. 🥀

He dated a girl from a strict religious family where appearance was treated as a moral failing. Showing her knees at 15 meant being shamed by her own mother, in language no teenager should ever hear.

This is how shame gets installed by the people who are supposed to protect you — and how childhood shame follows you into every relationship after.

If your family made you the problem for existing, that is what toxic family dynamics actually do, and naming it is the first part of letting go of shame.

MM 05:
At 27, Mark Manson made himself a rule: don't cheat, don't bail, don't create problems that aren't there. 💍

He'd been "a selfish piece of shit" and he knew it. So he wrote the agreement with himself: stay as long as there's no real problem. If there is one, leave. But if there isn't — don't invent one.

"It's gonna suck," he told himself. "But I'm gonna stick with it."

It is not a rule for staying in anything bad. It is a test for when to leave a relationship: a real problem, not an invented one. That is what commitment in a relationship costs, and nobody posts about the cost.

FO 05:
You can graduate top of your class and still be living at home for the next 10 years. He says that is what pushed a generation into trading. 🇰🇷

Se Yong Park on the @fomo stage at TOKEN2049 Singapore, on Korea specifically: the systems that worked for your parents and grandparents are not built for you. Be the best student, graduate top of the class — a job can still force you back to your parents' house for 5 to 10 years.

"That has created this environment where you want to find independence, you want to find your own path. And trading is maybe one of those things. I think content is another."

His point is not that trading is the answer. It is that people are hunting for any exit from a script that stopped working — a Korea job market that pays for credentials and not for independence.

Living at home in your 20s stopped being a personal failure and became the default. How to become financially independent is the question that whole generation is actually asking, and trading is one of the few answers that does not require a permission slip.

Did you leave home on schedule, or later than you planned? 👇

FO 06:
LeBron cannot teach anybody how to be LeBron. So why is everybody copying the freak of nature? 🏀

Ansem on the @fomo stage: the once-in-a-generation talent is useless as a blueprint, because nobody can repeat their path. The person worth studying is the one who had no idea and taught themselves anyway.

"Traders who have taught themselves how to trade... that's something that people can look up to and be like, oh, well, I could also be this person."

Relatability beats genius when you are choosing who to learn from. If you are looking for a trading mentor, the one worth copying is the self-taught one who had no map — because how to learn trading is a problem of sequence, not of talent.

FO 07:
Everyone writes NFTs off as dead. He says they are the most underrated thing in crypto. 🖼️

Ansem on the @fomo stage at TOKEN2049 Singapore. He concedes the whole case against them first: they were the fad of 2021, they came down fast and aggressively, and a lot of people lost money. Then he makes the actual argument.

"If you're gonna have a lot more businesses exist purely on-chain, then NFTs are a really good way to show ownership in those businesses and distribute revenues to people."

And the one nobody talks about: "NFTs are really good for forming community."

So the useful question is not are NFTs dead, it is what are NFTs used for once businesses live on-chain. Ownership, revenue distribution and community are the answers that survive the 2021 price chart.

Dead tech, or five years early? 👇
